idiom_name: explicit free/close on every exit path (goto cleanup tail) or GCC/Clang __attribute__((cleanup))
implementation_notes: C has neither destructors nor a framework Dispose contract, so release is a hand-written function (fclose/free/close/ReleaseMutex) that must be reached on every exit path; the classic C spelling is one goto-cleanup tail whose release sequence is guarded by NULL/-1 sentinels, which is how idempotence is obtained. GCC and Clang offer __attribute__((cleanup(cleanup_function))) on automatic variables: the function runs when the variable goes out of scope, in reverse definition order, on normal exit and - when -fexceptions is enabled - during stack unwinding, making it the closest local idiom to a disposer; it is a compiler extension rather than ISO C, does not work for static storage or parameters, and its own failure is undefined. An owner struct should still expose a single x_free() that cascades only to the handles it owns and clears them.
pitfalls: The cleanup function runs even when the variable was never assigned (a goto or switch that jumps over its initialisation), so initialise the pointer to NULL or make the callback tolerate it.
Reverse-definition-order execution is part of the contract: declare a resource before the one that depends on it, or the cleanup order will release the wrong thing first.
Portable C has no runtime safety net - a missed release leaks the descriptor until process exit and only ASan/valgrind will notice it.
